subject: 💰 Dems' economic test
body_html:
Plus: Productivity surge | Thursday, November 05, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Nov 05, 2026

Democrats' huge victory this week came on the back of promises to make life more affordable. Next comes the challenge of turning those promises into relief that voters can feel. More below.

  • Plus: encouraging signs on productivity growth. 📈

🇬🇧 Situational awareness: The Bank of England has officially joined the global rate-hiking cycle. The central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years, citing inflationary pressures stemming from the Iran war.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 1,064 words, a 4-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Democrats' affordability test
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Democrats won the midterms on voter frustration with high prices. Now they face the same problem that sank Republicans: Americans want lower prices, and there is little that policymakers can do to deliver them quickly.

Why it matters: Prices for necessities like groceries and gas can fall in a healthy economy. But the kind of broad price declines that would reverse years of price gains would likely come with job losses and falling incomes, leaving households worse off than before.

  • It sets up an early test for the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress and Democrats in statehouses across the country: delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets.

What they're saying: "Can you bring prices back to 2019 levels? No," Brendan Duke, senior director for federal budget policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, tells Axios. "But a lot of the price shocks are policy-induced, so there are ways that policy can reverse them."

  • Duke points to reversing food assistance cuts, restoring health insurance subsidies and ending the Iran war as possible sources of relief, with the "big, fat asterisk" that President Trump might not sign off.
  • Other economic problems — a potential rise in unemployment or the AI bubble bursting — could overshadow affordability without solving it, Duke says.

The big picture: Democrats have limited power over sources of pressure on household budgets.

  • Their midterm sweep helped lower oil prices through market expectations. But Trump still controls the next steps in the war, and further relief heavily depends on his next moves.
  • Congress could vote to repeal tariffs, potentially reducing costs for imported goods and American manufacturers. But as we wrote yesterday, Trump could simply veto that legislation (and more generally, there is no guarantee that businesses would pass all the savings on to consumers).
  • Plans to restore expired Affordable Care Act subsidies or reverse Medicaid cuts could hit a wall because of internal divisions or Trump's veto power, as our colleagues reported this morning.

The intrigue: Democrats who won big Senate races campaigned on bringing down prices, including proposals targeting groceries and gasoline.

  • James Talarico in Texas promised to lower grocery prices by rolling back tariffs and boosting competition. In North Carolina, Roy Cooper pledged to "make stuff cost less," while incoming Annie Andrews in South Carolina proposed suspending the federal gas tax.
  • Democratic victories in governors' races could produce a patchwork of state-level relief, including directly giving voters money: The governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, for instance, has proposed $1,500 rebate checks.

The other side: "'Affordability' seems to be the mandate for the new Democrat majority. So they need to either find a 'magic wand' to bring prices down quickly, or they need to ... give money to people (so the high prices are made 'affordable') yet again. Only causing more inflation," Jeff Gundlach, the billionaire investor and CEO of bond giant DoubleLine Capital, wrote on X yesterday.

What to watch: Prices don't have to return to their old levels for Americans to recover their purchasing power. That can come through a slower, less politically sexy process: wages growing faster than prices for a sustained stretch.

  • But that bets on the possibility that there won't be another inflationary shock. And it has been a tough decade so far for such a bet.

Reality check: For all the Democrats' Congressional gains, they do not control the executive branch, will not have veto-proof majorities and it's generally the president, not Congress, who takes the blame when people are unsatisfied with the economy.

  • Still, as Democrats look to win back the White House in 2028 and maintain congressional majorities, it would be nice to point to concrete action to help affordability.

2. Q3 productivity surge
 
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Productivity growth was strong in the third quarter, the latest sign that America's growth potential looks bright.

Driving the news: Output per hour of labor rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the July through September period, the Labor Department said this morning, the strongest in a year.

  • It follows three softer quarters of productivity growth that had cast doubt on a post-pandemic surge in businesses continuing to find ways to create more output from a finite labor supply.
  • Unit labor costs — how much businesses spend on labor for each unit of output they produce — fell at a 0.7% rate in Q3, a disinflationary sign that could reassure the Federal Reserve that price pressures are under control.

Reality check: Quarterly productivity data is volatile and can offer more noise than signal. Longer time horizons give a more reliable signal.

  • Over the last three years, labor productivity has risen at a 2.6% annual rate. It was higher than that in the 2022-2025 period, but the recent results easily surpass the roughly 1% annual productivity gains seen in the 2010s.
  • That should allow for stronger gains in growth and incomes over time, even as demographic change constrains the supply of labor.

The intrigue: The rising use of AI may be part of the productivity story, but given the surge started years ago, there's reason to think that it has more to do — for now, at least — with changes in work processes, more intensive use of capital and a burst of entrepreneurship in recent years.

  • Richard de Chazal with William Blair wrote in a note that there is "still-limited evidence that this represents a broad AI-driven productivity boom."
  • "Rather, we see much of the more recent improvement as being the result of post-COVID restructuring, efficiency gains, and capital deepening, as well as some early AI-related benefits," he added.

Of note: In its recent policy statements, the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee has said that productivity growth is "strong," but that didn't really align with the numbers in late 2025 and the first half of 2026.

  • The strong third-quarter result puts the data more closely in line with the Fed's description of the state of affairs.
